prompt: In the remediation of a dependency, which step does a dependency bot own?

choices.text: Judging whether the new version behaves
choices.why: That is the tests' job, and only as far as they reach.

choices.text: Proposing the change
choices.why: Right. It finds the newer version and writes the pull request; others decide whether it is right.

choices.text: Deciding whether an advisory still matters without the update
choices.why: That is a person's call, through lesson 7's gate and exceptions.

choices.text: Merging what passed
choices.why: A person merges, or a rule a person wrote; the bot only acts on that rule.

prompt: A bot proposes gunicorn's next minor release, and linkbox's pipeline passes. What has that pass not checked?

choices.text: That the lock installs with its hashes
choices.why: The test stage installs from the lock with `--require-hashes`, so that was checked.

choices.text: That the routes still answer
choices.why: linkbox's suite exercises every route, so that was checked.

choices.text: How the server now treats a slow client
choices.why: Right. No test exercises it, so a green pipeline says nothing about it.

choices.text: That the new version has no published advisory
choices.why: The composition stage checks exactly that.

prompt: Why can a version number not tell a bot that an update is safe to run?

choices.text: It states what its author claims changed, and the newest release is the least examined
choices.why: Right. Lesson 12's incidents include new versions that were the attack.

choices.text: Semantic versioning forbids security fixes in patch releases
choices.why: Patch releases are where most security fixes go.

choices.text: Package indexes publish versions without dates
choices.why: PyPI records an upload time for every file; the lesson's program reads them.

choices.text: A bot reads only the major number
choices.why: Both bots read the whole version, which is how they tell patch from minor.

prompt: zizmor reports `dependabot-cooldown` on the shortest `dependabot.yml`. What risk is the audit about?

choices.text: Too many pull requests opening in a single week
choices.why: That is the noise budget, which `schedule` and `groups` address; the audit is about age.

choices.text: A bad release proposed before anybody catches it
choices.why: Right. Several of lesson 12's incidents were releases bad for hours or days.

choices.text: Dependabot running with write permission on the repository
choices.why: The file has no permissions in it; that is a workflow question.

choices.text: Security updates arriving late
choices.why: The cooldown does not delay security updates at all.

prompt: linkbox's `dependabot.yml` waits 14 days. An advisory is published today for a pinned version, with a fix released yesterday. When does Dependabot propose it?

choices.text: In thirteen days, when the fix is fourteen days old
choices.why: That is the rule for version updates. Security updates do not wait.

choices.text: On the next scheduled Monday
choices.why: Like the cooldown, the schedule applies to version updates only.

choices.text: Never, because the release is younger than the cooldown
choices.why: It is proposed; refusing every young fix would leave the advisory open.

choices.text: As a security update, without waiting
choices.why: Right. The cooldown covers version updates only.

prompt: Why does linkbox's file keep major versions out of the Python group?

choices.text: Dependabot cannot group major versions
choices.why: It can; `update-types` was set to leave them out on purpose.

choices.text: Its failure would have many suspects
choices.why: Right. In a group, any update in it is a suspect when it fails; alone, a major's failure has one cause, and its changelog gets read.

choices.text: Major versions skip the cooldown
choices.why: They wait longer: `semver-major-days` is 30.

choices.text: zizmor refuses groups that mix update types
choices.why: zizmor has no audit about groups.

prompt: In `dependabot.yml`, the block that makes Dependabot wait before proposing a new release is called `___`.
After `npx renovate --platform=local` on the stale branch, `git status --short` prints nothing. Why?

choices.text: Renovate committed its changes
choices.why: No new commit appeared; the local platform makes none.

choices.text: It found nothing to update
choices.why: Its report listed four updates.

choices.text: Its local platform only reports
choices.why: Right. It is the mode for watching a bot decide without letting it act.

choices.text: It wrote its branches to the CI server
choices.why: Nothing was pushed; the CI server saw no run.

prompt: In the report on the stale branch, pluggy 1.7.0 shows `waiting: true` and werkzeug 3.1.9 does not. What separates them?

choices.text: pluggy's release is younger than `minimumReleaseAge`
choices.why: Right. Eight days old against fourteen required; werkzeug's had been public longer.

choices.text: werkzeug has an advisory and pluggy does not
choices.why: The local run read no advisories; it held pluggy back for its age alone.

choices.text: pluggy is a dev dependency, and Renovate waits on those
choices.why: The age rule applies to every file alike.

choices.text: The schedule allows only one update per Monday
choices.why: The schedule says when, not how many; that is `prConcurrentLimit`.

prompt: Why does the lesson run `renovate@44.164.10` rather than `renovate@latest`?

choices.text: The latest release needs a newer Node
choices.why: The version is pinned for repeatability, the same reason as lesson 15's pins.

choices.text: Several releases a day
choices.why: Right. With that many releases, `latest` would be a different program on every reading; a pinned tool behaves the same each time.

choices.text: `npx` refuses the tag `latest`
choices.why: `npx` accepts it; it is a choice not to use it.

choices.text: Older releases support the `local` platform only
choices.why: The platform exists in current releases too.

prompt: Nothing on the stale branch changed after it was compiled, yet the pipeline broke on it. Why?

choices.text: The composition stage times out on old locks
choices.why: It ran and gave a verdict with a reason.

choices.text: An advisory came out for werkzeug 3.1.8
choices.why: Right. It was published after the lock's date, with a fixed version. The verdict depends on the advisories known today, not on the lock alone.

choices.text: The tests do not support pluggy 1.6.0
choices.why: The test stage passed on that run.

choices.text: Branches other than main always fail the gate
choices.why: Every branch runs the same pipeline with the same rules.

prompt: After `pip-audit --fix`, `requirements.txt` says `werkzeug==3.1.9`. Why did the test stage break?

choices.text: The hashes under that line are still 3.1.8's, so the downloaded file matches none
choices.why: Right. The installer cannot tell a stale hash from tampering, so it refuses both.

choices.text: werkzeug 3.1.9 breaks one of linkbox's tests
choices.why: No test ran: the install failed first.

choices.text: pip-audit deleted `requirements.in`
choices.why: It left `requirements.in` untouched, which is a problem of its own.

choices.text: The gate refuses commits written by tools
choices.why: The gate reads advisories, not authors, and it never ran.

prompt: Put the runs of the stale branch in the order they happened, with the stage that decided each.
What does `-P werkzeug` add to the `uv pip compile` command that fixed the branch?

choices.text: It ignores the hashes for werkzeug
choices.why: The opposite: uv writes the new version's hashes.

choices.text: Only werkzeug moves
choices.why: Right. Every other pin stays as the file has it. The diff was the header and werkzeug's three lines.

choices.text: It pins werkzeug in `requirements.in`
choices.why: `requirements.in` was not touched.

choices.text: It upgrades every package to its newest release
choices.why: That is `--upgrade`; the other three old pins stayed old.

prompt: Which update does the lesson's table allow to merge with nobody looking?

choices.text: A minor release of Flask
choices.why: The tests cover the routes, not every behaviour a Flask release can change.

choices.text: A new base image digest
choices.why: Nothing tests the behaviour of the new operating system packages.

choices.text: A patch to pytest, after the cooldown
choices.why: Right. It runs only in the test stage, so passing tests are the whole judgement.

choices.text: A new commit of a pinned action
choices.why: Its code runs with the workflow's permissions and needs reading.

prompt: A team turns on auto-merge, but its bot's token can also push to `main` directly. What is wrong?

choices.text: Auto-merge needs the bot to have no token at all
choices.why: The bot needs a token to open pull requests; the problem is its reach.

choices.text: A direct push skips the checks
choices.why: Right. Auto-merge waits for the checks; a direct push never meets them.

choices.text: Pushes from bots are not recorded in the history
choices.why: They are recorded like anybody's; recording does not stop them.

choices.text: Auto-merge then merges majors as well
choices.why: What auto-merge accepts is set by its rules, not by the token.

prompt: Match each setting to the trade it makes.

pairs.right: fewer reviews, but a failure has several possible causes
proposals arrive together, later in the week
a bad release is likelier to be caught, and good fixes arrive later
no reviewer, so the pipeline is the whole judgement

right_distractors: security updates are delayed until Monday

prompt: `releases.py` counted linkbox's releases in the year to 16 October 2026. Grouped by week, how many pull requests would that year have needed?
A bot's pull requests start piling up unread. Which change does the lesson rule out?

choices.text: Grouping more updates together
choices.why: That is one of the remedies the lesson names.

choices.text: Batching the security updates monthly
choices.why: Right. The advisory-driven updates are the reason the bot exists; cut the noise, never them.

choices.text: Stopping minor updates of test tools
choices.why: The lesson names it as a way back inside the budget.

choices.text: Replacing a dependency that releases often
choices.why: Fewer dependencies is the cheapest budget, as lesson 15's third move.

prompt: Why does `releases.py` count transitive dependencies such as markupsafe and pluggy, which linkbox never names in a `.in` file?

choices.text: Transitive dependencies have more advisories
choices.why: The program counts releases, not advisories.

choices.text: PyPI lists them as direct dependencies of linkbox
choices.why: linkbox is not on PyPI; the program reads the requirements files.

choices.text: A bot proposes an update for every pin in the lock
choices.why: Right. The lock pins them, so each of their releases is a proposal.

choices.text: Without them the count would round to zero
choices.why: The direct dependencies alone released several times.

prompt: Which of these did the lesson actually run on your own machine? Choose every one.

choices.text: zizmor on `.github/dependabot.yml`
choices.why: Run, locally and in the pipeline.

choices.text: Dependabot opening a pull request
choices.why: Not run: Dependabot runs only on GitHub.

choices.text: Renovate with the `local` platform
choices.why: Run, and it wrote nothing.

choices.text: `pip-audit --fix` on the stale branch
choices.why: Run, and the pipeline broke on its result.

choices.text: Renovate merging its own pull request
choices.why: Not run: that needs a hosted platform.
